title: Judge begins sentencing Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault as prosecution calls for long jail term – latest updates
description:
Prosecuting barrister asks for a ‘category one’ sentencing length which ranges from 10 to 15 years

Proceedings are beginning now. Chief prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC is up on her feet. She’ll be the first to deliver remarks.

The sentencing has been pushed back as court staff attempt to rearrange the courtroom so one of the victims can be protected, PA reports.

Continue reading...
text: Brand sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault offences
Judge Bennathan asks Brand to stand up as he passes his sentence judgement.
He says the sentence for rape is nine years imprisonment.
The total sentence is 10 years, six months, with the sexual assault offences.

Key events3m agoBrand sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault offences8m ago'You thought fame meant you could act however you liked'36m agoChannel 4 worker assaulted by Brand said attack was 'brushed under the carpet'42m agoVictim says Brand has 'no remorse' for his behaviour2h agoRecap2h agoBrand's lawyer: 'We invite mercy'2h agoDefence says anal rape 'a short and momentary failure' by Brand2h agoDefence barrister argues Brand's crimes were 'isolated incidents'3h agoProsecutors request 10 to 15-year sentence for rape conviction3h agoProsecutor says Brand's crimes caused 'severe psychological harm'3h agoBrand's public profile meant 'he remained present in my life' after rape, says victim3h agoRape victim abandoned comedy dream, abused alcohol to cope after attack3h agoVictim felt she was 'damaged goods' after Brand attack, she tells court5h agoBrand could face further charges5h agoBrand arrives in prison van for sentencing5h agoBrand denied bail after conviction5h agoBrand's convictions5h agoBrand to be sentenced for rape and sexual assault today
The judge says with the mitigating factors in play, he will reduce his sentence for Brand by a year.
He has not given the full sentence yet.
Judge Bennathan has repeatedly called Brand a sexual predator during his address so far.
He notes mitigating factors of no crimes having been reported in the past 17 years, and some evidence testifying to Brand’s character.
'You thought fame meant you could act however you liked'
The judge, laying out the crimes, notes Brand’s “staggering arrogance” and how his entourage regularly indulged Brand’s actions.

Three of the four crimes took place in public settings, in front of other people – at a bar, radio station and a setting where an advert was being filmed. Others in the room laughed after the assaults, the women said.
double quotation markThese insults in front of an audience, said after the assault amount to an additional humiliation.

double quotation markThe whole episode reeks of casual disrespect, and your belief that fame meant you could act however you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live.
The judge is relaying the sexual assaults Brand committed against the women.
He starts with the attacks on one woman in a pub in London where Brand groped the breast of a fellow party attendee.
“The effect on her had her wandering the streets of London, phoning a friend in the middle of the night, tearful and distressed.”
He outlines another assault, where Brand, visiting a radio station with an entourage launched himself at a woman, groping and kissing her in front of her colleagues and his entourage.
He notes the attack’s impact on her, how it damaged relationships with her male colleagues.
“There was the added humiliation of you assaulting her in front of an audience and the laughter afterwards”.
Judge Bennathan starts with Brand’s climb to fame 20 years ago.
“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic.
“You had also become a sexual predator,” he says.
“Your status protected you until 2023 when journalists published allegations” about his rapes and sexual abuse of women.
Such public reporting “empowered” other women to come forward to police, says Bennathan.
Judge Bennathan is about to begin his sentencing remarks, having considered the submissions from the prosecutor and Brand’s defence lawyer this morning.
A reminder that Russell Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile actor-comedians, was convicted last Thursday of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

A jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six women on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
The legal counsel are starting to file back into the courtroom. Justice Joel Bennathan has said he will deliver his sentencing remarks at 2pm.
Reporting from Southwark Crown Court
Brand has sat upright and remained remarkably composed throughout the trial, but he was seen looking down at his lap towards the end of this morning’s hearing.
When he left the dock, he could be seen clutching prayer beads in his right hand and nodding at his wife, Laura.
She seemed emotional when Ian Winter KC told the court she was standing by him.
“Words are completely inadequate… to convey the total devastation she’s experiencing,” he said.
Channel 4 worker assaulted by Brand said attack was 'brushed under the carpet'
Brand was convicted last week of forcing himself onto a woman in a Channel 4 radio studio, kissing her and groping her.
In her victim impact statement the woman says she spoke up immediately after the attack but it was “brushed under the carpet by senior management”.

“This really affected me and had something similar happened again at that time, I know I would not have had the confidence to speak up again. There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore.”
She said she felt powerless in the moment. “It had a knock-on effect on my confidence because I felt like I had no control on that day and there was nothing I could do about what he did to me.”

She said giving evidence in court “to a room full of strangers and Russell Brand took me right back to how I felt on the day of the assault. It was a hugely distracting and overwhelming process and it took an awful lot out of me.”
“I am eternally grateful to the police and prosecution team for their support and for allowing my voice to be heard.

“I finally feel believed but I am still so anxious. I worry that there will be repercussions for telling the truth. This was and is being spoken about so much by the world media and social media, it’s left me feeling exposed and exhausted.”
Victim says Brand has 'no remorse' for his behaviour
One of Brand’s victims was assaulted by him at her workplace, attacked in a small room at the offices of Capital Radio in 2009.
Her victim impact statement was read out by Karmy-Jones:
double quotation markRussell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse for how his behaviour has impacted my life. I just hope that he is not allowed to hurt any more women.
She relayed how Brand had “managed to move on and even forget that he sexually assaulted me violently in a very public place and in front of people.”
“This has had a lasting impact on my life even if I thought that I had successfully buried what happened.

“I recognise this now but I tried for so long to be strong and carry on- business as usual. However over the years hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction, especially to his voice.”
She was diagnosed with severe anxiety 20 years later, after the first published reports about Brand’s actions against women were published.

“It was the first time in 20 years that I had spoken to anyone about what had happened. I almost decided to withdraw from the case as I did not think I was strong enough emotionally to proceed with my allegation.” But she persisted with bringing a case to police, with the support of the detectives and officers who took her case seriously she said.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC has asked Judge Bennathan for a category one sentence – where prison terms begin at 12 years, but have a range of 10-15 years depending on aggravating or ameliorating factors.
But she noted too that if the court didn’t agree with that category, the next level down, a category two sentence would have a starting point of eight years, with a range of seven-nine years.
Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter KC, pushed for a much more lenient punishment, a sentencing between category two and three.
Another detail revealed during Brand’s lawyers argument earlier was that one of the character testimonies given to the court came from the woman at the centre of the ‘Sachsgate’ scandal.
Brand built a career, partly based on this image where he would brag about his sexual exploits and pursuits of women.
In 2008, he was the host of a BBC show where and Jonathan Ross left voicemails on Fawlty Towers actor Andrew Sachs’ phone, saying that Brand had slept with Sachs’ grand-daughter Georgina Baillie.
Brand subsequently left the BBC after the disgraceful prank and Ross was suspended.
Now, it’s been revealed that Baillie was one of six people who gave character references in support of Brand. She said he had helped paid for her alcohol rehab programme.
Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter read out some of her statement:“I still choose to support him as a person I know him to be.”

I’m just going to run through some other details the prosecution highlighted as “aggravating” factors, when presenting the case to the judge that Brand should receive the most serious category one level of sentencing.

In the case of the rape – where Brand removed his condom and anally penetrated a then-21-year-old fan at his home and then dismissed her afterwards, calling her “dirty” in follow-up messages – the prosecutor argued Brand knew of the young woman’s idolisation of him and abused that position of trust.
His victim was worried for months afterwards that she may have contracted HIV from him.
Karmy-Jones KC noted how he had pursued conversations with the “vulnerable young woman,” offering her advice on the problems she was having with her boyfriend at the time.
When Brand learned that she and her boyfriend had separated, he told her he would look out for her, that he would hold her.
“The court will wish to consider whether this introduces an element of abuse, of trust and manipulation”, said Karmy-Jones.
A quick recap of the arguments both sides have made. Brand’s lawyers are looking for a more lenient sentence, the prosecution has called for serious category one term.

Karmy-Jones KC pushed for Brand to receive a sentence of 10-15 years for the rape conviction, arguing that his crimes warranted such a level of punishment because of how he had abused his position, and then further degraded and humiliated his victims.
She said Brand had the view that he could abuse without impunity and he must bear some responsibility for the culture around him which enabled his offending for years.

Karmy-Jones read out three victim impact statements from the women abused by Brand. All described the debilitating impacts of his violence, and how it had damaged their relationships, careers, their feelings of self-worth and confidence and their day-to-day existence.
One woman delivering her statement in person to the judge. She said she had carried around “that undeserved feeling of shame” for 20 years.
All of the victims said they still carried the trauma with them to this day, and relayed the stressful experience of going to court to bring him to justice.
Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter KC, argued that Brand was a fundamentally changed man these days.
He said the crimes had occurred 17 years ago, and had been “isolated incidents”. He described the rape that Brand has been convicted for as a “short and momentary failure” of consent.
Winter said any major sentence given out to Brand would have a “catastrophic” impact on his young family and urged Judge Bennathan to show mercy.
Both arguments have been made now. The judge has now adjourned to court to go and consider his sentencing decision.
He will be back at 2pm to deliver his remarks, which will be televised.
Winter is speaking at length about Brand’s rehabilitation and his religious care efforts in recent years.

He had concluded an earlier section of his argument by beseeching the judge to pass the sentencing judgement on the basis of Brand’s good character. He called Brand a “fundamentally different person today” and has pointed out the rapes and sexual assaults he has been convicted of took place 17 years ago.

“There is a side to Mr Brand that very few people know about,” he says, and notes that “a large number of people” have come forward to the defence team speaking of his good deeds. But he admits none of them wanted to go on the record or tell a court of this.

Winter concludes by urging the judge to sentence Brand, who he says is not the “monster portrayed outside this courtroom”, and to consider the “catastrophic” impact his jailing will have on his young children.
